lesson.title: Disruption in the Oval Office: The Trump Presidency
lesson.summary: Donald Trump's two nonconsecutive terms, beginning in 2017 and resuming in 2025, brought a norm breaking, social media driven communication style and some of the sharpest partisan approval gaps of any modern presidency.
lesson.body:
Donald Trump, a real estate developer and reality television personality who had never held elected office, won the 2016 presidential election against Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton and was inaugurated as the 45th president on January 20, 2017. His first term ran through January 2021, and he was elected again in 2024, returning to office on January 20, 2025, as the 47th president, only the second person in American history, after Grover Cleveland in the 1880s and 1890s, to serve two nonconsecutive terms.

Trump's first term included several significant policy actions. In 2017 he signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, a major reduction in individual and corporate tax rates. His administration pursued stricter immigration enforcement, including a travel ban restricting entry from several majority Muslim countries and efforts to build additional barriers along the U.S. Mexico border, and it imposed tariffs on goods from China and other trading partners as part of a broader trade dispute. Trump withdrew the United States from the Paris Climate Agreement and from the Iran nuclear agreement, and he appointed three justices to the Supreme Court, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett, shifting the Court's ideological balance.

Trump's communication style was itself a significant part of his presidency and connects directly to the era's changes in social media and political discourse. He used Twitter extensively to announce policy, criticize opponents and the press, and speak directly to supporters without going through traditional media filters, a practice that supporters saw as authentic and transparent and critics saw as norm breaking and at times inflammatory. This made him one of the clearest examples of how social media had changed the relationship between political leaders and the public since the platforms' rise in the mid-2000s.

The House of Representatives impeached Trump twice, a first in American history. In December 2019 he was impeached on charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress related to a phone call with Ukraine's president, and the Senate acquitted him in February 2020. After he lost the November 2020 election to Joe Biden, Trump and many allies made repeated claims, which state and federal courts and his own administration's election security officials found no credible evidence to support, that the election had been stolen through fraud. On January 6, 2021, a crowd of his supporters, after a rally near the White House, stormed the U.S. Capitol in an attempt to disrupt Congress's certification of the electoral vote, resulting in the House impeaching Trump a second time, this time for incitement of insurrection; the Senate again acquitted him, in February 2021, after he had already left office. Trump remains one of the most closely and consistently studied examples of political polarization in modern American history, with approval ratings that split more sharply along party lines than almost any other recent president, a pattern examined more closely in the study of political polarization itself.
